Scoring cheat sheet

For each sign that is true, add its points → total 0–10. 6+ = flagged (must include a serious sign below).

High priority6–10 + serious sign
Watch closely3–5
Keep monitoring0–2

Serious sign = after a cancelled order, customer placed no new order for 30 days (+2) · higher-price same-driver loop. 60 days is checked in section ⑦ to confirm they really left — it does not add points. ("No other driver took it" is no longer scored — it happens about as often for normal drivers, and the harm it points to is already caught by "Customer lost".)

Spotting cheat-app (bot) drivers — who to check by hand

Scope — HK truck · public-pool · 30d

More ▾

This page is about 610 cheat-app (bot) drivers. We looked at all public-pool truck drivers (van / mudou / mudou9; company orders left out), then kept the 610 who run a bot. Almost every order they released is On Demand (91% On Demand, 5% Same Day, 4% Next Day). Data pulled 2026-07-23, covering 30 days (24 Apr – 24 May 2026).

How we count (read this once)

More ▾
Released vs cancelled — Released = driver took the order then released it (event_type_cd = 4, actor_type = 'Driver'). Cancelled = the order later ended with no driver (status = 'cancelled', cd 8 or 11) — used in sections ⑤⑦. Scored pool needs ≥1 release, not a cancelled count.
Who gets a score — 30d cohort (24 Apr – 24 May 2026): must took ≥30 orders (orders_assigned_30d), finished ≥30 (orders_completed_30d), and released ≥1 order (releases_by_driver_30d). If any rule fails → outside_analysis_pool (not scored yet; can still work).
Orders (booking-type mix on the top) — for the On Demand / Same Day / Next Day share only: each order counted once. That mix is not used in the +1 / +2 steps below.
Lost-customer steps (sections ⑤⑦) — bot pool only (610 drivers). We add up each driver’s counts from the mart (released_orders_90d → released_then_no_driver_90d → customer_no_return_30d_90d). Step 1 total = 19,249. If two bot drivers both released the same order, that order can appear twice in the sum — that is fine. All % in ⑤⑦ use this same sum so they match BigQuery.

🤖 Step 1 — spot the cheat-app bots (grab-and-drop speed) — how we spot bots

More ▾

Before looking at any harm, first find who is running a bot. The one thing a human hand cannot fake: grabbing and letting go of several different orders within a few seconds. For each driver we take their busiest 8 seconds and count how many different orders they grabbed and let go, across all three booking types (On Demand, Same Day, Next Day) — not On Demand only (BQ: max_distinct_grace_drop_orders_in_any_8_seconds_30d, column bot_speed_tier).

Most grab-and-drops in any 8 seconds

scored drivers (30d · 24 Apr – 24 May 2026) · bar = drivers · right column = grace-drop orders (driver_drops_order_30d, cd=21) in the same cohort

3+ in 8 seconds = a machine. A human tapping fast does 1, at most 2. At 3+ the count falls off a cliff — only 31 drivers (1%). No human hand grabs and dumps 3 different orders in under 8 seconds → confirmed bot.
Bot review pool = 610 drivers. Confirmed bot (3+): 31 — act. Suspected bot (2): 579 — also review. Together 610 of the 3,041 scored drivers in this slice go into the bot pool. Everything below (customer lost, cherry-pick, higher-price loop) is what they did with the bot — harm comes after detection, it is not how we spot the bot.

Step 1 (bot detection). Each step filters drivers (not orders). Bar 1 = everyone we checked. Bar 2 = met minimum activity rules (enough orders to analyse — not a bot test). Bar 3 = bot pool by grab-and-drop speed (2+ in 8 seconds). Columns: meets_minimum_activity_rules, bot_speed_tier.

Bot spotting vs harm scoring — two separate checks

More ▾

Bot spotting ends at the bot pool (bar 3). The funnel answers “who is running a bot?” — 610 in the bot pool (31 confirmed at machine speed; see Step 1 above). ③ Harm tiers below then answers, within this bot pool only: “how much harm did each bot driver cause?” — a 0–10 score from lost customers, higher-price loops and cherry-picking. Bot speed = detect the pool; the score = rank the damage inside it.

⑤ Warning signs, and how many drivers show each

Each sign adds points to the warning score. Counted among the 610 bot pool drivers. Cancelled after release is common and usually harmless, so it no longer adds points. Same customer gone for 30 days = +2 — numbers and how serious → ⑦. Higher-price loop = +3 → ⑧. Cheap trips dropped more often = +1 → ⑨.

⑥ Which warning signs travel together (do X → also do Y)

Do these warning signs show up alone, or do they often happen together? Read across a row: of drivers who have the row sign, what share also have the column sign. Darker = more often together.

Of drivers who do ROW, % who also do COLUMN

each cell = % of the row's drivers who also show the column sign · darker = higher

What it means (in one glance)

These signs are not random — they often show up together. When a driver grabs the customer's re-order (the loop), 89% of them also had an order cancelled because no other driver took it, and 34% had a customer with no new order for 30 days after that cancelled order (among pool drivers with the loop sign).
So the loop is not a one-off. It usually comes after the same bad pattern: release the order → nobody else takes it → (sometimes) the customer stops ordering → same driver grabs the higher-price re-order.

⑦ Definition: "Customer lost" (+2) — what it means and how serious it is

In one line: order cancelled after a release is common → +1. Same customer places no new order for 30 days → real loss → +2. 60 days only checks they really left — it does not add points. Numbers below = bot pool only (610 drivers), 24 Apr – 24 May 2026.

Why +1 vs +2 — step by step (bot pool) Step 1 — driver released an order (event_type_cd = 4): 19,249 times (we add up each bot driver’s releases).
Step 2 — nobody else took it → order cancelled: 1,445 (7.5% of Step 1). Common. Usually the customer comes back → only +1.
Step 3 — that same customer is gone: 184 placed no new order for 30 days (12.7% of Step 2). Real lost customer → +2.
Check (no points): 89% (164 of 184) still had no order at 60 days.

Chart below: how active those lost customers were in the 90 days before they left — describes value only; score stays a flat +2 (same for HIGH or NONE).

The 184 lost customers, by orders in their 90 days before

mart sum across bot pool drivers (churn_cust_recent_*_90d) · darker = more active before they left

So this is NOT "just throwaway new customers"

About 1 in 4 were active customers. MEDIUM + HIGH = 47 (26%) were placing 3 or more orders in the 90 days before, then stopped. On average a lost customer had placed ~1.85 orders in the prior 90 days. Losing them is real damage.
And they really left. 89% of these lost customers (164 of 184) still had no new order at 60 days after that cancelled order. Only 11% came back — mostly on days 31–60. (60-day check does not change the +2 score.)

⑧ Definition: higher-price same-driver loop (+3) — why it scores highest

Higher-price same-driver loop = the driver released an order → the customer re-ordered the same trip at a higher price (new GTV > old GTV) → the same driver took that new order and finished it. It scores +3 (a strong sign) because the same person both killed the first order and then earned the more expensive re-order — a closed money loop (self-enrichment). Column: same_driver_reorder_priced_up_flag.

What must all be true

miss any one step → no +3

1 · Driver releases the order The driver took the order, then released it.
2 · Customer re-orders the same trip — more expensive New order GTV (gross_transaction_value) is higher than the old one. Same price or cheaper does not count.
3 · Same driver takes it back and finishes The same driver_id accepts the new order and completes it. Taking it back but not finishing does not count.

Why this gets +3

Same person, both sides of the deal. One driver made the first order die, then earned the higher-priced re-order and finished it. That is a closed money loop — not bad luck, not “another driver happened to take it.” A cheat app cannot do this — the bot only grabs and dumps orders fast; the loop is a human gaming the rules.
Price must go up — or it is not self-enrichment. Only when the new trip costs more (new GTV > old GTV) do we treat it as the driver benefiting from releasing the order. Same price or cheaper does not get +3. Among the 610 bot pool drivers: 14 higher-price same-driver loops were found (same_driver_reorder_priced_up_90d summed across bot pool drivers) · 13 drivers with the loop sign. (queried 2026-07-23, HK TRANSPORT public-pool candidates, mature cohort 24 Apr – 24 May 2026)
Highest points because intent + benefit line up. This is a strong sign for human review (alongside customer lost). If the same loop happens two or more times in the 30d cohort, add a separate +1 booster (same_driver_reorder_repeat_flag) — not a gate.

BQ: same_driver_reorder_priced_up_flag (+3) · same_driver_reorder_repeat_flag (+1).

⑨ Cheap trips get dropped more often (+1)

In one line: they keep expensive trips and drop cheap ones — more than similar drivers. That is +1. Helper only — not enough alone to flag for hand review.

Three checks (all must pass)

miss one → no +1

1 · Drop cheap, keep expensive Trips they drop are usually cheaper than trips they finish. We use the typical price (not the average), so one airport trip does not break the rule. Need at least 5 drops and 3 finished trips in 30 days.
2 · More than similar drivers They drop more often than drivers with the same vehicle and same membership (van Bronze vs van Bronze — not vs mudou Platinum).
3 · Both true → +1 58 of 610 bot-pool drivers hit this. (queried 2026-07-23, HK TRANSPORT, 24 Apr – 24 May 2026)

Remember

+1 is a helper, not a verdict Busy areas also raise drop rates. One point alone never puts a driver in the top review band.
We score “drop after take” — not the free 8-second cancel The free quick cancel is for spotting bots. Harm scoring looks at when they take a trip then let it go — that can leave the customer waiting.

BQ: released_median_gtv_below_completed_flag (+1 price only) · released_order_abnormal_flag (+1 = price + more than peers).

⑩ Two real drivers — what they actually did, step by step

Two worked examples, not the scoring rule (the rule is the checklist on the right). One driver runs a bot; the other has human hand speed but games the rules to make more money. We went through their real orders step by step so you can see exactly what earned the warning.

Same-driver loop — driver 103819 (score 8)

Tai Tong → Shek Lei · GTV $150 → $193 (+$43) · 2026-04-28 (times HKT)

Not a bot — this driver has human hand speed. It shows a person gaming the rules by hand, so you can tell it apart from the bot below.

What this does NOT say — read before acting:
  • A review list, not a verdict. It goes to Ops + Trust & Safety to check by hand. No penalty is recommended here.
  • No dollar figure yet. How much money we lost (net_impact_hkd) needs the LTV model — not built. Until then, no punishment.
